Compressed sensing

Words: 1k Articles: 19
Sparse optimization OurBigBook.com
Compressed sensing reconstructs a sparse vector, or an approximately sparse one, from fewer linear measurements than its ambient dimension. Basis pursuit replaces counting nonzero coordinates by convex ℓ1 minimization. A null space property characterizes exact uniform recovery, while a robust null space property controls errors from noise and nonsparse tails.

Coherence of a normalized matrix (μ(A)=maxi=j​∣⟨ai​,aj​⟩∣)

Words: 165 Articles: 2
Compressed sensing OurBigBook.com
For a matrix with at least two columns of unit Euclidean norm, its mutual coherence is the largest magnitude of an inner product between distinct columns. It measures the strongest pairwise ambiguity of linear measurements. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives 0≤μ≤1. The order-two restricted isometry constant equals the mutual coherence, because every two-column Gram matrix has eigenvalues 1±∣⟨ai​,aj​⟩∣.
Cumulative coherence (μ1​(k)=maxi​max∣S∣=k, i∈/S​∑j∈S​∣⟨ai​,aj​⟩∣)
Words: 117 Articles: 1
Coherence of a normalized matrix OurBigBook.com
For unit Euclidean norm columns, cumulative coherence measures the largest sum of k correlations with one other column. Its domain is 0≤k≤N−1, with μ1​(0)=0 by the empty-sum convention. It is nondecreasing, μ1​(1)=μ for N≥2, and μ1​(k)≤kμ, where μ is the mutual coherence. Keeping a sum of actual correlations can be substantially sharper than replacing each summand by the largest one.
Cumulative coherence bound for restricted isometry (δs​≤μ1​(s−1)≤(s−1)μ)
Words: 54
Cumulative coherence OurBigBook.com
For normalized columns and 1≤s≤N, the restricted isometry constant is bounded by the cumulative coherence at s−1. A restricted Gram matrix has diagonal one and every off-diagonal row sum at most μ1​(s−1). The Gershgorin circle theorem and the finite-dimensional spectral theorem bound its eigenvalues between 1−μ1​(s−1) and 1+μ1​(s−1). At s=1 the distortion is zero, and at s=2 it is exactly the mutual coherence.

Sparse injectivity

Words: 67
Compressed sensing OurBigBook.com
A linear map is injective on the class of sparse vectors of order s exactly when its null space contains no nonzero vector with at most 2s nonzero entries. Differences of two sparse vectors have at most 2s active coordinates. Conversely, splitting the support of a vector of a 2s-sparse null vector into two parts constructs two distinct s-sparse vectors with the same image. The strict null space property implies sparse injectivity by applying it to both parts of such a split.

Restricted isometry property

Words: 134 Articles: 2
Compressed sensing OurBigBook.com
The restricted isometry property controls ∥Ax∥22​/∥x∥22​ uniformly over sparse vectors. It supplies quantitative near-orthogonality of disjoint sparse coordinate combinations, not merely normalization of individual columns.
Restricted isometry constant (δs​(A))
Words: 110 Articles: 1
Restricted isometry property OurBigBook.com
The order-s restricted isometry constant is the smallest nonnegative δ satisfying (1−δ)∥x∥22​≤∥Ax∥22​≤(1+δ)∥x∥22​ for every vector with at most s nonzero coordinates. Equivalently it is max∣S∣≤s​∥AS∗​AS​−I∥2→2​. The sparse-vector quantifier is essential, and the constant can equal zero.
Sharp order-s restricted-isometry recovery theorem
Words: 72
Restricted isometry constant OurBigBook.com
For s≥2 and δ=δs​(A)<1/3, noisy basis pursuit has error ∥x^−x0​∥2​≤C1​η+C2​σs​(x0​)/s​, with constants depending only on δ. One admissible pair is
C1​=1−3δ22(1+δ)​​,C2​=1−3δ22​(2δ+(1−3δ)δ​)+2(1−3δ)​.
(123)
These constants follow from Theorem 3.3 of the sharp restricted-isometry recovery analysis, with the actual noise bounded by the tolerance η. The restriction s≥2 is necessary: equal unit columns give δ1​=0 without unique recovery. The coefficient of the approximation term cannot universally be one.

Basis pursuit (min{∥x∥1​:Ax=y})

Words: 525 Articles: 7
Compressed sensing OurBigBook.com
Basis pursuit minimizes an ℓ1 norm subject to exact linear measurements. Basis pursuit with a noise tolerance replaces the equality by ∥Ax−y∥2​≤η. A unique minimizer has linearly independent active columns, and hence at most rankA nonzero coordinates: a null direction on its support would make the objective locally affine on a feasible line, contradicting minimality or uniqueness.
Strict dual certificate for basis pursuit (AS∗​h=sgn(xS​),∥ASc∗​h∥∞​<1)
Words: 160 Articles: 1
Basis pursuit OurBigBook.com
For a real vector x with support of a vector S, this certificate is a vector h whose measurements under the adjoint operator match the active sign function values and lie strictly between minus one and one on the inactive coordinates. If AS​ is injective, such a certificate proves that x is the unique basis pursuit minimizer. For a nonzero v∈kerA, injectivity ensures vSc​=0, and 0=⟨A∗h,v⟩ implies the fixed-sign null space condition. The strict inequality is interpreted coordinatewise if Sc is empty. The condition with the sign function written here is for real variables; complex basis pursuit uses the unit phases of active coordinates instead.
Least-norm dual certificate (h0​=AS​(AS∗​AS​)−1sgn(xS​))
Words: 70
Strict dual certificate for basis pursuit OurBigBook.com
When AS​ is injective, this vector solves AS∗​h0​=sgn(xS​). Any other solution differs by a vector in kerAS∗​, orthogonal to the range of AS​ containing h0​. The Pythagorean identity therefore proves that h0​ has the smallest Euclidean norm. It is a strict dual certificate for basis pursuit exactly when each inactive coordinate of A∗h0​ has magnitude less than one. Failure of that test does not rule out another certificate: a null space component of AS∗​ can alter those inactive coordinates.
Nullspace property
Words: 308 Articles: 4
Basis pursuit OurBigBook.com
The null space property relative to S is ∥hS​∥1​<∥hSc​∥1​ for every nonzero h∈kerA. It is equivalent to exact basis pursuit recovery of every vector supported in S. Sufficiency follows from the triangle inequality; for necessity, compare −hS​ and hSc​, which have the same image under A. Recovery of a single fixed signed vector can hold without this uniform property.
Lq null space property (∑i∈S​∣vi​∣q<∑i∈/S​∣vi​∣q)
Words: 147 Articles: 1
Nullspace property OurBigBook.com
For 0<q≤1, this strict inequality for every nonzero v∈kerA and every ∣S∣≤s is equivalent to unique constrained ℓq recovery of every sparse vector of order s. For sufficiency, use ∣xi​+vi​∣q≥∣xi​∣q−∣vi​∣q on the support of a vector. For necessity compare x=−vS​ with vSc​, which have the same measurements. The statement concerns uniform recovery over the whole sparse class, rather than a single signed vector.
Monotonicity of uniform sparse recovery in the exponent
Words: 84
Lq null space property OurBigBook.com
If the Lq null space property holds at q≤1, it holds at every 0<p<q. Order a nonzero null vector's magnitudes a1​≥⋯≥aN​ and put t=as​>0. Since p−q<0, the top-s p-power sum is at most tp−q times its q-power sum, while the tail p-power sum is at least that multiple of the tail q-power sum. The strict q inequality therefore gives the strict p inequality. The largest s magnitudes are the worst support of a vector, so all other supports satisfy it too.
Robust null space property (∥hS​∥2​≤ρ∥hSc​∥1​/s​+τ∥Ah∥2​)
Words: 57
Nullspace property OurBigBook.com
The displayed property holds for every h and every ∣S∣≤s, with 0≤ρ<1 and τ>0. It converts the cone inequality from basis pursuit minimality and the tube inequality from noisy feasibility into a two-constant bound ∥x^−x0​∥2​≤C1​η+C2​σs​(x0​)/s​. Both constants are needed in general; a fixed coefficient one on the approximation term does not follow.
Fixed-sign null space condition
Words: 43
Nullspace property OurBigBook.com
For a real vector x0​ with support S, uniqueness in basis pursuit is equivalent to ∣⟨sgn(x0,S​),hS​⟩∣<∥hSc​∥1​ for every nonzero h∈kerA. The supporting-line inequality for the absolute value proves sufficiency. Taking small positive and negative multiples of h before any active sign changes proves necessity.

Sparse vector (∣suppx∣≤s)

Words: 203 Articles: 3
Compressed sensing OurBigBook.com
A vector is s-sparse if it has at most s nonzero coordinates. For x∈RN, its best s-term ℓ1 approximation error is σs​(x)=minz s-sparse​∥x−z∥1​, equal to the sum of the absolute values of the coordinates outside the largest s.
L0 sparsity count (∥x∥0​=∣suppx∣)
Words: 63
Sparse vector OurBigBook.com
The number of nonzero coordinates of a finite vector is its L0 sparsity count. It vanishes only at zero, but is unchanged under multiplication by a nonzero scalar, so it is not a norm. Minimizing it under linear measurement constraints finds a sparse vector with the smallest possible support of a vector. Sparse injectivity of order s guarantees unique recovery of every sparse vector with at most s nonzero coordinates by this objective.
Support of a vector (suppx)
Words: 98 Articles: 1
Sparse vector OurBigBook.com
The support of a finite vector is the set of indices of its nonzero coordinates. It is the support of a function on a finite discrete index set, and its cardinality defines sparsity.
Maximum-support vector in a finite-dimensional subspace
Words: 69
Support of a vector OurBigBook.com
For any field F and vector subspace W⊆Fm, some u∈W has at least dimW nonzero coordinates. Choose u with largest support of a vector S. Restriction from W to FS is injective: a nonzero vector in its kernel of a linear map vanishes on S, so adding it to u would enlarge S. Thus dimW≤∣S∣. The argument works over finite fields, where assuming a generic vector avoids finitely many hyperplanes would be invalid.

Linear stability domain

Words: 929 Articles: 15
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
For a one-step method applied to y′=λy, write yn+1​=R(hλ)yn​. Its linear stability domain is
S={z∈C:∣R(z)∣≤1}.
(124)
Forward Euler has R(z)=1+z, while backward Euler has R(z)=(1−z)−1 and is A-stable.

Strict linear stability domain (Ddecay​={z:yn​→0})

Words: 67
Linear stability domain OurBigBook.com
The strict decay convention for a linear stability domain demands that every numerical mode tends to zero on the Dahlquist test equation. For a one-step stability function it requires ∣R(z)∣<1; for a multistep method it requires every amplification root to have modulus below one. This differs from a boundedness convention that allows simple unit-circle roots, and from mesh-uniform finite-time numerical stability. Cambridge numerical analysis notes use the decay convention. Explicitly specifying the convention is essential for methods with undamped modes.

A-alpha stability (A(α))

Words: 35
Linear stability domain OurBigBook.com
A numerical time-stepping method is A(α)-stable if its absolute stability region contains the negative-axis sector {z:∣arg(−z)∣≤α}, for 0<α≤π/2. With a stability function R, this requires ∣R(z)∣≤1 throughout that sector. At α=π/2, this is A-stability.

Euler method (yn+1​=yn​+hf(tn​,yn​))

Words: 284
Linear stability domain OurBigBook.com
The Euler method approximates an initial value problem y′=f(t,y), y(t0​)=y0​, by evaluating the derivative at the current point and moving along that tangent line for a time h. With tn​=t0​+nh, its displayed update needs one evaluation of f per step. This simple rule turns local slope information into a whole approximate trajectory. MIT's course notes derive it by dropping the second-order Taylor remainder.[ref]
Take y′=−2y, y(0)=1, whose exact solution is the exponential function y(t)=e−2t. The Euler method gives
yn+1​=(1−2h)yn​,yn​=(1−2h)n.
(125)
At h=0.2, the first values are 1,0.6,0.36,0.216. At t=1, five steps give 0.65=0.07776, compared with e−2≈0.135335. The result decays but is too small: absolute stability alone does not ensure accuracy. At h=1.2, the first values are 1,−1.4,1.96,−2.744, and at t=6 five steps give −5.37824, while the exact solution is about 0.00000614421.
For the Dahlquist test equation y′=λy, the Euler method has stability function R(z)=1+z with z=hλ. Its absolute stability region is ∣1+z∣≤1, the closed disk centred at −1 with radius one. For the present real decay problem and h>0, bounded numerical values require 0<h≤1; strict decay requires 0<h<1. At h=1 the values alternate 1,−1,1,… without decay. These conditions follow directly from the amplification factor 1−2h, matching MIT's criterion for y′=−ay.[ref]
The Euler method is first order: with bounded second derivative and suitable Lipschitz continuity, its global error is O(h) on a fixed interval. In this example the logarithm gives log(1−2h)=−2h−2h2+O(h3) for small positive h. At t=nh, this means yn​=e−2t(1−2th+O(h2)). It explains both the downward bias and why halving the step roughly halves the error once h is sufficiently small.

A-stability

Words: 388 Articles: 8
Linear stability domain OurBigBook.com
A method is A-stable when its stability domain contains the closed left half-plane.

A-stability of near-diagonal exponential Padé approximants (n−2≤m≤n)

Words: 65
A-stability OurBigBook.com
For nonnegative degrees m,n with n−2≤m≤n, the [m/n] Padé approximant R to the exponential function has no poles in the left half-plane and satisfies ∣R(z)∣≤1 for Rez≤0. Consequently a numerical method having that stability function is A-stable. In particular, the near-diagonal choice [s−1/s] gives the Radau IIA method stability function, while [s/s] corresponds to the Gauss collocation method. The theorem concerns these exponential approximants, not arbitrary rational approximations with the same degrees.

Principal-root obstruction to A-stability (Relogw(z)>0 for some Rez<0)

Words: 75
A-stability OurBigBook.com
Suppose a consistent linear multistep method has a simple principal polynomial root and its analytic logarithm satisfies logw(z)=z+Cz2r+O(z2r+1) near zero, with real coefficients. If C(−1)r>0, then at z=iε the real part of logw is positive to leading order. The same remains true after giving z a small negative real part of smaller magnitude than that leading term. Thus a growing amplification factor occurs inside the left half-plane, ruling out A-stability. For an order-three method with C>0, choose z=−Cε4/2+iε.

Explicit multistep methods cannot be A-stable

Words: 52
A-stability OurBigBook.com
For an explicit linear multistep method, the highest-degree coefficient of ρ(w)−zσ(w) is fixed while at least one lower coefficient grows unboundedly with negative real z. If all roots stayed in the unit disk, the elementary symmetric polynomials of those roots would keep every monic coefficient bounded. This contradiction proves that no nontrivial consistent explicit method is A-stable.

Boundary-locus test for multistep A-stability (z(θ)=ρ(eiθ)/σ(eiθ))

Words: 76
A-stability OurBigBook.com
A unit-modulus amplification root of a linear multistep method puts its test-equation parameter on this boundary locus, except when numerator and denominator both vanish. If the locus avoids the open left half-plane, the leading coefficient never vanishes there and the roots are initially inside the disk at one point there, continuity keeps them inside throughout that connected region. Checking zero-stability, imaginary-axis roots and common polynomial factors is still necessary. A boundary plot alone is not a proof of A-stability.

An A-stable one-step method is L-stable when its stability function also satisfies R(z)→0 as ∣z∣→∞ within the left half-plane. It damps modes whose decay time is far shorter than the numerical step.

Midpoint method

Words: 34
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
The midpoint method advances an ordinary differential equation using a derivative evaluated at a temporal midpoint. Its explicit form predicts that midpoint from the initial derivative, while the implicit midpoint rule solves for the derivative at the mean of the endpoint states.

Collocation method

Words: 31
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
A collocation method chooses an approximate solution from a finite-dimensional trial space and forces the residual of a differential equation to vanish at selected nodes. Collocation Runge-Kutta methods apply this principle to polynomial approximations on each time step.

QR algorithm

Words: 23
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
The QR algorithm computes eigenvalues through repeated QR decompositions and similarity updates. Shifted and unshifted forms have different convergence rates; the unshifted QR algorithm uses a zero shift at every step.

Iterative method

Words: 31
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
An iterative method approximates a solution by repeatedly updating an initial guess. In numerical linear algebra, a stationary iterative method for a linear system uses a fixed iteration map; other iterations can change their update rule or search space at each step.

Forward error (x−x∗​)

Words: 46
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
The forward error is the difference between a computed result x and the exact result x∗​ for the original data. Its size can be measured by a norm, or relative to ∥x∗​∥ when x∗​=0. A linear-system residual measures the equation imbalance instead; the condition number relates that imbalance to the forward error.

Backward error (δd)

Words: 54
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
A backward error measures a perturbation δd of the input data for which the computed result is an exact solution of the perturbed problem. Specify which data may change and which norm measures the perturbation. For a linear system Ax=b, holding A fixed gives δb=Ax−b, the negative linear-system residual. The corresponding forward error also depends on the condition number.
